Choosing backing patterns by genre

The style of a song comes mostly from the rhythm section: how the bass, the chords and the drums divide the beat. This article shows which patterns fit which genre, and how to keep a repeated pattern from sounding mechanical.

Contents
  1. How the three parts work together
  2. Combinations by genre
  3. Notes on each genre
  4. Making it sound less repetitive

How the three parts work together

  • Drums set the grid: the hi-hat (or ride) shows the smallest note value — 8th notes in an “8-beat”, 16th notes in a “16-beat” — and the snare on beats 2 and 4 is the backbeat most pop and rock is built on.
  • Bass connects the drums and the chords. It usually plays the root on beat 1 together with the kick drum, and moves to the next chord with passing notes.
  • Piano (or guitar) fills in the harmony. Busy rhythms (8th notes) push the song forward; long notes (whole notes, broken chords) leave space for the voice.

When one part is busy, the others usually play less. A busy 16-beat drum pattern with a busy piano and a busy bass sounds crowded.

“Shuffle” is the app's Shuffle setting: Off = straight 8ths, On = a triplet shuffle. Tempo ranges are rough guides, not rules.

Notes on each genre

Rock

Steady 8th notes in the bass and the piano, with the kick on 1 and 3 and the snare on 2 and 4. For a chorus that lifts, switch the drums to the ride cymbal pattern and add a fill at the end of the verse.

Pop

Syncopation — notes that land just before the beat — gives pop its bounce. The piano pattern with anticipation plays the next chord half a beat early; the syncopated bass and a 16-beat or tambourine groove fit with it.

Ballad

Leave room for the voice: whole notes in the bass, broken chords in the piano, a soft cross-stick on the snare. The 8th-note arpeggio with a 3-3-2 left hand gives a gentle push without crowding the melody.

Soul / R&B and funk

The bass moves more (octaves, fifths and approach notes), and the drums play 16th notes with ghost notes on the snare. An electric piano or a clavinet sound suits these styles.

Hip-hop and dance

Electronic kits (808, 909) and synth bass. Dance music usually has a kick on every beat (four on the floor) and a clap on 2 and 4; hip-hop keeps the kick syncopated and leaves space.

Shuffle, blues and jazz

These are played with a swung (triplet) feel, so set Shuffle to On. A walking bass plays one note per beat, mostly chord tones and scale steps, and often approaches the next chord's root by a half step. In jazz the ride cymbal carries the time and the piano “comps” — short chords in between the melody.

Making it sound less repetitive

  • Variation. Real players change small things every few bars. Variation adds bass runs and piano anticipations, crashes at the start of phrases and short lead-ins at their ends (4- and 8-bar phrases).
  • Fills at section ends. Put a fill (Snare 16ths (1 beat), Tom run (2 beats), Tom run (1 bar) …) on the last bar before a new section.
  • Change the pattern between sections. For example a quieter pattern in the verse and a fuller one in the chorus. If a single bar needs something special, edit that bar only.
  • Feel. A little feel (timing and velocity differences) makes the parts sound played rather than programmed.
